items.title: GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN VOCATIONAL UNDERGRADUATE FINANCE AND ACCOUNTING EDUCATION: APPLICATIONS, RISKS, AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is entering finance and accounting classrooms before curricula, assessment systems, and institutional controls have fully adapted. This narrative review explains the technical principles of large language models and examines their use in vocational undergraduate finance and accounting education. Potential applications include dialogic tutoring, formative feedback, text simplification, case simulation, spreadsheet and programming support, financial analysis, professional communication, and course design. These functions can make practice more accessible and provide rapid opportunities for comparison and revision. Their educational value, however, depends on how the task is structured. Fluent output may contain fabricated facts, obsolete rules, incorrect calculations, biased assumptions, or unsupported recommendations. Unrestricted assistance may also improve immediate task performance without developing the independent knowledge and professional judgment that students need. Additional concerns include academic misconduct, confidential-data exposure, unequal access, unreliable detection, and weak accountability. A responsible integration model should therefore separate AI-free foundations, guided AI assistance, and AI-critical professional tasks. It should require authoritative-source verification, calculation checks, process records, disclosure, reflection, and oral or practical defense. Future systems may combine domain-controlled retrieval, multimodal simulations, and auditable learning records, but vocational programmes need direct longitudinal and multi-institutional evidence. Generative AI should be treated as a supervised learning partner and an object of professional evaluation, not as an authoritative answer engine.

items.title: Global patent landscape of security and policing innovations: Trends, networks, and emerging technologies
items.abstract: Security, as both a phenomenon and a practice, faces challenges from cyber threats and global terrorism, driving rapid technological innovation, as evidenced by patent filings. This study analyses 27,913 patents from 1993 to 2023 on national security and policing technologies from WIPO’s Patentscope. Using mixed methods, especially statistical tests using SPSS, network analysis using Gephi and thematic coding using NVivo, the study identifies inventor networks, jurisdictional trends and emerging technologies. Results show a post-2014 growth in surveillance, data processing and large-scale Machine Learning technology, with the US and China leading the Innovation. The final finding calls for balanced global policies on innovation and ethics, laying down a pathway for future security research. Method: The study retrieved data from the Patentscope database of the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO) in Geneva and analysed patent filings in national security and policing technologies spanning 1993 to 2023. Through inclusion and exclusion criteria, 27,913 out of 31,359 patent records were considered for analysis. This Study undertakes a mixed-method approach, i.e., descriptive statistical analysis, chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis Tests in SPSS, network analysis in Gephi, and thematic analysis in NVivo. Results: The study found a significant increase in the number of innovations since 2014, with the majority of contributions from the US and China. At a prima facie level, the advancement in innovation in law-and-order tools for surveillance, data processing, and communication technologies is evident. Towards the later phase, a new shift has emerged in areas like artificial intelligence and quantum computing, signalling a revolution for security providers. Conclusion: The article highlights the importance of technological progress in strengthening global security frameworks and appeals to the international bureaucracies to formulate policies that balance innovation and ethical considerations. These findings may help policymakers, researchers, and security experts gain insights to shape future security strategies.

items.abstract: This paper derives a neutral factorization invariant and identifies the conditions required to recoverthe Explicit-Tacit separation used by the Formal Reasoning and Feedback Protocol (FRFP). Correctness ismodeled by an independently specified family of semantic distinctions and its canonical quotient. Thefactorization criterion requires a nonempty semantic domain. Lean verifies the repaired factorization core, itsprincipal downstream propositions, an injection form of the finite-string boundary, selected countermodels andworked witnesses, and the conditional semantic and representational core of the recovery theorem. It does notverify the empirical P0 protocol or instantiate and discharge the FRFP-specific comparison obligations.Countermodels show that finite naming, failure of a current representation, world-state unevaluability, andunrestricted representation are individually insufficient to induce a nontrivial modal distinction. The analysisseparates the aggregate correctness quotient from item-level contents and specifies a typed comparisoninterface whose image I_C is the domain of any FRFP modal comparison. Because modal information may besmuggled into the boundary between semantics and presentation, the interface-freeze gate constructs a sampledfamily of admissible anchor/surface partitions, requires necessity and ablation evidence for semantic features,varies the cue surface within each partition, and tests interface and verdict invariance across the family. Blindedmapping and adversarial leakage assessment consume the frozen suite. Boundary sensitivity yields onlypartition-dependent reconstruction; a predictive but semantically inseparable cue makes independent recoveryunidentifiable from the present source. Recovery is formulated as four obligations: two align correctnesssemantics and two align representation spectra on I_C. Discharging the gate and these obligations suffices forextensional agreement with FRFP Explicit/Tacit modality; the paper does not claim that they have beendischarged against the FRFP Lean specification. items.title: Governing medical AI under the EU AI Act: an integrated compliance-by-design framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important component of healthcare, supporting diagnosis, clinical decision-making, medical imaging, triage, and patient-facing services. While these technologies offer significant opportunities to improve healthcare delivery, they also raise important questions about patient safety, fairness, privacy, transparency, cybersecurity, and accountability. This paper examines the regulatory framework governing medical AI in the European Union, focusing on the interaction between the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act), the Medical Device Regulation (MDR), the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Device Regulation (IVDR), the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and the European Health Data Space (EHDS). Drawing on doctrinal and conceptual regulatory analysis, it argues that many AI-enabled medical systems should be regulated through continuous lifecycle compliance rather than by relying primarily on a one-time assessment at market entry. The analysis identifies the training and validation dataset as a particularly important point of regulatory convergence, especially among the EHDS, GDPR, and AI Act data-governance requirements, and examines how responsibility is allocated across the general-purpose AI value chain under Article 25. Building on this analysis, the paper proposes a compliance-by-design framework that translates overlapping legal requirements into a set of auditable governance artefacts covering system classification, regulatory mapping, data governance, validation, human oversight, conformity assessment, post-market monitoring, and change control. The framework is illustrated through two contested use cases and complemented by recommendations tailored to the responsibilities of different stakeholder groups. The analysis incorporates Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Digital Omnibus on AI), while recognising that supporting guidance, harmonised standards, and implementation of the EHDS continue to evolve and should be checked when the framework is applied. The framework is conceptually derived and illustrated through constructed use cases rather than empirically validated; future work should assess its usability, consistency, and discriminating power through structured expert assessment and Delphi-based consensus methods.
